responses.response: Follow a top-down process: start with C1 to define the system boundary, actors, and external systems; then move to C2 to identify the runtime or deployable containers and their interactions; then add C3 only for containers that are complex, risky, or central enough to need internal detail. Add Dynamic views and Deployment views only after the structural model is stable, and treat both as optional and targeted rather than mandatory. Do not start bottom-up from classes, folders, or frameworks.

No—C3 is not mandatory for every container. Keep the C1→C2 progression, and only add C3 when a container is complex, architecturally central, risky, or hard to understand from C2 alone. If your API container is simple and already well explained at C2, stop at C2 and skip the detailed C3 view.

That is not correct for C1. A C1 view must stay static and show the system boundary, actors, and external dependencies; it is not for step-by-step or temporal flow. Put the user journey in `views 'Use Cases'` as a dynamic view instead, because dynamic views are the right place to show ordered interactions between the user, web app, and API over time.

First re-establish the workspace rules and active project context with `understand-project-structure`, especially in an unfamiliar LikeC4 workspace. Then confirm or reconstruct the C1 boundary so you know which system, actors, and external systems the new work belongs to. After that, design the C2 model by identifying the containers and their typed interactions. Use `create-element` for container declarations, `create-relationship` for relationship kinds and labels, and `design-view` for the actual C2 view; finish with `test-model` to validate the result.

This skill should not detail everything itself; it is the sequencing and orchestration layer. Since your C2 already exists, keep C1 and C2 as the stable core, then add the nominal user scenario as an optional dynamic view using `create-sequence-view`, and add the production infrastructure as an optional deployment model using `model-deployment-infrastructure`. In short: use this skill to decide order and scope, and hand the detailed flow and deployment work to the specialized skills.

Start by revalidating the active project and shared specs with `understand-project-structure`, because shared changes can affect kinds, relationships, and view organization in a multi-project workspace. Then do a quick C1/C2 sanity pass so you do not jump straight into details blindly. If the target container still truly needs deeper detail, add the C3 view next—using `create-element`, `create-relationship`, and `design-view` for the detailed structural edit. After the structural model is stable, document the nominal user scenario with `create-sequence-view`, and finish with `test-model` to verify the updated model.
